sections.h2: Where is Hancock County, Mississippi, and what is in it?
sections.html:
Hancock County sits on the Gulf of Mexico at the Louisiana line, and its county seat is Bay St. Louis. It covers 553 square miles, but 79 of them (14%) are water, which tells you how much of the county is bayou, bay and marsh.

The three cities are Bay St. Louis, Diamondhead and Waveland. Kiln and Pearlington are census-designated places, and smaller communities include Lakeshore, Clermont Harbor, Necaise and Napoleon. The county is part of the Gulfport-Biloxi metropolitan area and is the home of the John C. Stennis Space Center, which Wikipedia describes as NASA's largest rocket engine test facility.

sections.h2: How did Hurricane Katrina change Hancock County housing?
sections.html:
Katrina made its final landfall here on August 29, 2005, and the county's own history is the main reason local sellers talk about storm damage first. Wikipedia's county article reports that not one building or home was left intact along the 7-mile beach front, that nearly the entire first block off the beach was destroyed, and that homes as far as 10 miles inland flooded.

Highway 603 south of Interstate 10 was submerged and the Highway 90 bridge at Bay St. Louis was wrecked. Bay St. Louis, Waveland, Pearlington, Diamondhead and Kiln all took heavy damage. Ask any seller of a coastal house how it fared in 2005, because buyers will.

For a seller this has practical meaning:

  • A buyer's insurer and lender will ask about flood zone and elevation, and a house with past water damage can be hard to finance.
  • With 14% of the county's area covered by water, many parcels sit near the shore, so ask the county or FEMA flood maps where yours falls.
  • A cash buyer who purchases as-is can skip the repair and insurance hurdles that sink conventional contracts, but should still be told about any known damage.

sections.h2: Who assesses and collects property tax in Hancock County?
sections.html:
Hancock County combines the jobs: the County Administrator also serves as Tax Assessor and Collector, according to the Mississippi Association of Supervisors. The Hancock Chamber of Commerce lists the office at 854 Highway 90 in Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 466-5791, and the county's own Tax Assessor page links to tax and fee information and a homestead exemption page.

  • Board of Supervisors: 854 Highway 90, Suite A, Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 467-0172.
  • Chancery Clerk and land records: 854 Highway 90, Suite B, phone (228) 467-5404.
  • Appeals of an assessment go to the Board of Supervisors, with the Chancery Clerk as the contact.

We could not open the pages that give Hancock's payment methods, office hours or interest rate, so we are not stating them. Call the office before you pay or mail a check.

sections.h2: What does the state say about Hancock County tax rates and classes?
sections.html:
Every Mississippi county uses the same constitutional classes, and the tax equals true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate. The county, each city and the school district set their own levies, which is why a house in Diamondhead and a house in unincorporated Kiln can see different bills.

ClassPropertyRatio
IOwner-occupied single-family home10%
IIOther real property15%
IIIPersonal property15%
IVPublic utilities30%
VMotor vehicles30%

The Department of Revenue posts combined county and city millage rates for 2012 through 2025 on its property tax data page, which is the place to look up an official number for Hancock County. We have not copied a rate here because we did not open that file. Real property must be revalued at least every four years, and the assessor does not have to enter your home to do it.

sections.h2: When are Hancock County property taxes due?
sections.html:
The state due date is February 1, and the tax is assessed to whoever owns the parcel on January 1. Bills are issued in November and December, and a February 1 that lands on a weekend or holiday rolls to the following Monday with no penalty or interest.

If taxes stay unpaid, real property can be offered at the county tax sale. Counties choose between the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August, and we did not find which one Hancock uses on a page we could open. After a sale, the owner has two years to redeem under Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3, as summarized in Mississippi Supreme Court opinions. Property nobody buys goes to the State and is handled by the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637.

In practice, sellers should ask for a current payoff and any prior-year balance before they sign a contract. A title company will not close until delinquent taxes are cleared.

sections.h2: How do I contest a Hancock County assessment?
sections.html:
Request a hearing before the Board of Supervisors, using the Chancery Clerk as your point of contact. The Department of Revenue says an appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the taxes are due, so a homeowner who disagrees with a value cannot wait for the bill in December.

Bring evidence. Storm damage or a wrong square footage on the record are examples of facts worth documenting. The state notes that a refund for prior years can be possible when an appraisal had inaccurate information about home size, and the Chancery Clerk can explain how.

sections.h2: Do homestead exemption and age rules affect a Hancock County sale?
sections.html:
They do, because a buyer who plans to live in the home must apply in their own name. Applications go to the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and the state says you do not reapply each year unless your status changes.

Owners 65 or older, and totally disabled owners who otherwise qualify, are exempt from taxes on the first $75,000 of true value. Eligibility is lost if the owner or spouse is out of compliance with state income tax laws or tags a vehicle in a different county from the home. A seller who has moved out should not keep claiming homestead on a house they no longer occupy.

sections.h2: What do Hancock County sellers usually face?
sections.html:
Sellers here may be dealing with a home that has storm or flood history, an inherited property or a house that has been vacant. Each situation has its own paperwork:

  1. Pull the deed and last tax statement and confirm the current owner on the roll.
  2. Ask the Tax Assessor and Collector for any prior-year balance.
  3. Confirm with the Chancery Clerk that no tax sale is recorded on the parcel.
  4. Gather repair and insurance records so a buyer can price the house honestly.

A cash sale lets the buyer take the house as it stands, and we make no promise on price. This page is general information, not legal or tax advice, so confirm every figure with the county office.

faqs.q: When are Hancock County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due on or before February 1 under state law. If that date is a weekend or legal holiday, you can pay the following Monday without penalty or interest, according to the Mississippi Department of Revenue.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Hancock County?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessor and Collector, a combined office headed by the County Administrator. The Hancock Chamber of Commerce lists it at 854 Highway 90, Bay St. Louis, phone (228) 466-5791. Call to confirm hours and payment methods.

faqs.q: How do I appeal a Hancock County assessment?
faqs.a: Ask the Board of Supervisors for a hearing, with the Chancery Clerk as the contact. The state says an appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax is due.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Hancock County house damaged by a storm?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a damaged house as-is. You still need clear title and any taxes paid or settled at closing, and you should disclose damage you know about.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem a Hancock County parcel after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Two years from the date of the tax sale, according to Mississippi Supreme Court opinions citing Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3. The Chancery Clerk handles redemption notices and payments.
